title: Choosing friends
hook: a person is on the religion of his close friend (Abu Dawud)
tomorrow: why would an angel stop a man on his way to see a friend?

segments.voice: Yesterday, pray together: a grandson on the Prophet's back, and a grown-up who waited. Today, the people you choose, not the ones you're born to.

A new group chat full of strangers, all headed to the same campus in the fall. Within an hour, smaller chats split off. Where you land matters more than it looks. The Prophet ﷺ told it as a scene at a market. You're walking between two stalls. On one side, a perfume seller. On the other, a blacksmith pumping his bellows. You haven't bought anything. You're just standing there. And already something is happening to you.
screen: `A NEW GROUP CHAT.` → `TWO STALLS IN A MARKET.` → `YOU HAVEN'T BOUGHT A THING.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene as Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it. The perfume seller might give you some for free. Or you might buy some. And even if you do neither, you walk away smelling good. The blacksmith's bellows might burn your clothes. And even if they don't, you walk away smelling of smoke. That, the Prophet says, is a good companion and a bad one. Nobody has to say a word. It gets on you. A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud says it outright: a person is on the way of their close friend, so look carefully at whom you take as a close friend. The word is khalil, the close friend, not everyone in the group chat. You can be kind to a whole class and still choose your inner few with care. And the perfume isn't a label. It's what rubs off: patience, honesty, a friend who reminds you it's time to pray, or tells you the truth when it stings. The blacksmith isn't a villain, either; he's working. The question is only what you carry home on your clothes. One to tell a friend tonight: in the Prophet's picture, you don't have to buy anything to come home smelling of it.
screen: `PERFUME, EVEN IF YOU DON'T BUY.` · `SMOKE, EVEN IF YOU DON'T BURN.` · `KHALIL: THE CLOSE FRIEND.` · `WHAT RUBS OFF ON YOU.` · then, large: `CHOOSE FRIENDS WELL.`

segments.voice: If there's anything with a scent near you, soap, coffee, a sleeve that still smells of someone's house, hold it close and breathe it in. Notice how it stays a little after you set it down. Then bring to mind one friend whose goodness has rubbed off on you, and name to yourself exactly what they left on you.
screen: `ONE SCENT, BREATHED IN.` · `WHAT STAYS AFTER.` · `ONE FRIEND'S PERFUME.`

segments.voice: Choosing friends: picking your close few with care, because what they carry gets on you. Perfume, or smoke.
Your line: choose friends well, because by evening it's in your clothes. That's five of ten.

screen: `DAY 1716 COUNTS.` → `FAMILY AND FRIENDSHIP · 5 OF 10.` → `TOMORROW: WHY STOP A MAN ON HIS WAY TO A FRIEND?`

howItsDone: Muslims quote the perfume seller and the blacksmith when talking about friends, and speak of good company, suhba, as something that shapes faith over time.

fork.setup: a new teammate is hilarious but mocks anyone who studies. a quieter one always helps you prep. who do you sit with on the long bus ride?
options: the funny one; friends are mostly for a good time.
neither; keep to yourself so nothing rubs off.
the one who helps you prep, and stay friendly with both.
fork.reveal: the parable isn't about shutting people out; it's about where you stand longest. kind to everyone, close to the perfume.

original.note: Arabic: a close friend, an intimate; the word in the Abu Dawud hadith.

trapdoor: what you thought: choosing friends means avoiding anyone different.
what it means: choose your close few by what rubs off on you: perfume or smoke.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 2101 gives the parable of the perfume seller and the bellows; Abu Dawud 4833 says a person follows the way of their khalil.

making friends only with people like you
keeping as many friends as you possibly can

chat.says: chicago chats are splitting into groups. do i only join the MSA one and skip the rest?
options: Join widely, choose your close few with care. The hadith is about your khalil.
Only the MSA. Anyone outside it will slowly change your religion.
Join everything equally. If your faith is strong, friends don't matter.
chat.meaning: The hadith says to look carefully at your close friend, your khalil. Kind to many; careful with the few who rub off on you.

Sahih al-Bukhari.meaning: a major collection of reports of the Prophet's words and deeds

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2101 (also 5534; the perfume seller and the blacksmith's bellows)
Sunan Abu Dawud 4833 (a person is on the religion of their close friend, so look at whom you befriend)

notes: Bukhari 2101 and Abu Dawud 4833 (also Tirmidhi 2378): confirm numbering, grading and paraphrases. 'Way' renders din in the Abu Dawud hadith (the outline says 'religion'); a Keeper may prefer 'religion'.
'The perfume isn't a label' and 'kind to a whole class' are the lesson's reading of the parable as about character; it doesn't say whom Muslims may befriend. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable.
